author: blu
body: The elliptic-curve kinds are separate variants and not one variant with a curve field beside it, for the same reason X25519 is separate from Ed25519: a field can be ignored and a variant cannot.

author: blu
body: What a certificate says it was signed WITH, which is a different question from what its own key is FOR. It used to be a Boolean called xc-sig-ed25519 that was set to True without reading anything, so every certificate in the world claimed to be Ed25519-signed and the one branch that consulted it refused all the ones that were not.

author: blu
body: This one is now the signature AlgorithmIdentifier's check and nothing else. It used to admit an OID parameter too, because it was shared with the key path, and that shared leniency was the hole: an elliptic-curve key could carry ANY named curve and the curve was never read.

author: blu
body: The question the chain walk asks, and the reason the algorithm is typed: an X25519 key must never be handed to a signature verification.

author: blu
body: It lives in this chapter rather than in the chain walk because it is DER decoding and this is the DER-decoding chapter, and because it has two callers: a certificate's signatureValue and a TLS CertificateVerify signature are the same encoding, and RFC 8446 section 4.4.3 says so explicitly for ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256. It was written in X509Chain first, when the chain walk was its only caller.

author: blu
body: The width is the CURVE's, passed in, not a constant. It was 32 until 2026-07-28, which would have refused every P-384 signature on the length test below rather than on anything to do with the signature: r and s are forty-eight bytes there, and `> 32` is None.
